title: Behind on Mortgage Payments Options: What Homeowners and Investors Need to Know
excerpt: Falling behind on mortgage payments can feel overwhelming, but there are more options available than most people realize. This guide breaks down every path forward — for struggling homeowners and the savvy investors who can help them.
author: AIWholesail Team
metaDescription: Explore all behind on mortgage payments options including loan modifications, forbearance, short sales, and how investors can find motivated seller deals.

sections.content: Missing a mortgage payment is one of the most stressful experiences a homeowner can face. Whether it happens because of a job loss, medical bills, divorce, or just a slow month, the anxiety that follows can make it hard to think clearly. The good news? There are far more behind on mortgage payments options than most people know about — and acting quickly makes a huge difference in the outcome.

This guide is written for two audiences: homeowners who need a way out, and real estate investors who want to understand the landscape so they can find motivated sellers and create win-win deals. Whether you are the one behind on payments or you are looking to help someone in that situation, understanding every option available is the first step.
Why Acting Early Changes Everything

Most lenders do not start formal foreclosure proceedings until a borrower is at least 120 days past due. That window — roughly four months — is critical. During that time, homeowners have the most leverage and the most options. Once a Notice of Default is filed, choices start to narrow and legal costs begin to pile up. A homeowner who is just one payment behind has dramatically more flexibility than one who is six months in. If you are a real estate investor searching for pre-foreclosure leads, the early-stage distressed homeowner is also where the best deals tend to live.

Pro Tip: If you are behind even one payment, call your lender before they call you. Lenders are legally required to provide information about available loss mitigation options, and many have hardship programs that never get advertised publicly.
Option 1: Loan Forbearance

Forbearance is an agreement between you and your lender to temporarily pause or reduce your mortgage payments. It does not erase what you owe — you will need to repay it later — but it buys you time to get back on your feet. During COVID-19, millions of homeowners used forbearance plans, and the process has since become more standardized. Most forbearance periods last between 3 and 12 months. After the forbearance ends, your lender will typically offer a repayment plan, a loan modification, or a deferral of the missed payments to the end of your loan.
Option 2: Loan Modification

A loan modification permanently changes the terms of your mortgage to make it more affordable. This might mean a lower interest rate, an extended loan term (say, from 20 years remaining to 30 years), or rolling your missed payments into the back end of the loan. For example, a homeowner with a $1,800 monthly payment might get it reduced to $1,450 through a modification — a difference that makes staying in the home possible. Modifications require documentation of your financial hardship and typically take 30 to 90 days to process. You can find a breakdown of how different financing terms affect monthly payments using our free [Mortgage Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/mortgage-calculator).
Option 3: Refinancing

If you have equity in your home and your credit is still in reasonable shape, refinancing into a new loan with better terms can lower your monthly payment significantly. This option works best for homeowners who are just one or two payments behind and have not yet seen major credit score damage. Keep in mind that most lenders require you to be current on your mortgage to qualify for a traditional refinance, so timing matters. Some hard money and private lenders offer refinance products specifically for distressed borrowers, though these usually come with higher rates.
Option 4: Selling the Home

For many homeowners, selling is the cleanest way out — especially if they have equity. A traditional sale through a real estate agent can net the most money, but it takes time. If the home needs repairs or the homeowner needs to close in weeks rather than months, selling to a cash buyer or real estate investor is often the faster, smarter path. Investors in active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) regularly buy homes from distressed sellers quickly, often covering all closing costs and allowing sellers to walk away without further damage to their credit.

'The worst thing a homeowner can do when they fall behind is nothing. Every option available shrinks the longer you wait.' — Housing counselor insight widely shared in HUD-approved counseling programs.
Option 5: Short Sale

A short sale happens when the lender agrees to accept less than the full amount owed on the mortgage as payment in full. This is typically used when the home is underwater — meaning the homeowner owes more than the property is worth. Short sales require lender approval and can take 60 to 120 days, but they are far less damaging to your credit than a foreclosure. A foreclosure can stay on your credit report for seven years and drop your score by 100 to 150 points. A short sale, while still negative, is generally treated more favorably by future lenders.
Option 6: Deed in Lieu of Foreclosure

A deed in lieu of foreclosure means you voluntarily hand the property back to the lender in exchange for being released from the mortgage obligation. It avoids the lengthy and public foreclosure process and is slightly less damaging to your credit than a full foreclosure. Lenders are not always eager to accept this option — they often prefer a short sale — but in cases where the property has little market value and no other buyer is available, it can be a workable solution. Some lenders also offer a cash-for-keys incentive of $1,000 to $3,000 to encourage homeowners to leave the property in good condition.
For Investors: How to Find and Help Homeowners Behind on Payments

Pre-foreclosure and mortgage-distressed properties represent one of the most consistent sources of below-market deals in real estate investing. Homeowners in these situations often prioritize speed and certainty over maximum price — which creates real opportunity for investors willing to move quickly and offer fair, transparent solutions. The key is approaching these situations with empathy. You are solving a real problem for a real person, not just chasing a discount.
How to Find Pre-Foreclosure Leads

items: Check public county records for Notices of Default (NODs) — these are public filings and updated regularly
Use list-pulling services that filter by mortgage delinquency, equity position, and property type
Drive for dollars in neighborhoods with older housing stock or visible deferred maintenance
Work with probate attorneys, divorce attorneys, and bankruptcy trustees who interact with distressed sellers
Partner with real estate agents who specialize in short sales and pre-foreclosure listings

sections.content: What to Offer a Homeowner Behind on Payments

When you approach a homeowner who is behind, lead with solutions. Explain the options available to them — forbearance, modification, short sale, cash sale — and let them choose what fits their situation. Many do not know these options exist. If they want to sell, a cash offer with a 7-to-14-day close can be life-changing for someone facing imminent foreclosure. Make sure you understand the numbers: what they owe, what the property is worth as-is, and what repairs are needed. Our guide on [Financing for Real Estate Investors](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-financing) can help you structure creative offers that work for both parties.

Pro Tip: Subject-to deals — where you take over the existing mortgage payments without formally assuming the loan — can be a powerful tool when the homeowner has a low-rate loan. Always consult a real estate attorney before structuring a subject-to transaction.
A Quick Decision Framework

items: 1 to 2 payments behind + good credit + equity → Try refinancing or loan modification first
3 to 4 months behind + equity + needs to move fast → Cash sale to an investor is often the best path
Underwater on the mortgage + income reduced → Explore short sale or deed in lieu
Temporary hardship with steady job → Forbearance and repayment plan is likely the right fit
No equity + no income + lender won't negotiate → Consult a HUD-approved housing counselor for free at 1-800-569-4287

sections.content: No two situations are identical, and the best option depends on how far behind the homeowner is, how much equity exists, what the local market looks like, and what the homeowner's long-term goals are. Markets like Phoenix, Dallas, and Atlanta have strong investor demand, which means cash buyers are readily available and deals can close fast. In slower markets, traditional lender workouts may be the more practical route.
